source.title: Value Residual Learning
source.authors: Zhan-Chao Zhou; Tian-Yi Wu; Zhiyun Jiang; Fares Obeid; Zhen-Zhong Lan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation losses for different architectures at fixed model size, bearing on whether architecture details change loss. It does not reproduce or fit the scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss sweeps over model size and training tokens, but does not fit power laws or report exponents. These sweeps therefore do not establish the power-law form or small-run extrapolation. It cites scaling laws and uses the Kaplan et al. data-size relation when choosing its dataset size; those cited results and the sizing formula are not new results of this study. Downstream scores are reported, but not as a test of predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper. It proposes ResFormer and SVFormer and reports their validation loss against Transformer, NeuTRENO, DenseFormer, GQA and CLA. It uses scaling-law results only as tools: Kaplan's D ≥ 5000·N^0.74 to size the 20B-token dataset, a fixed 10,000 steps, and a summed-learning-rate remark. It fits no power law and runs no extrapolation or compute-optimal analysis. Its fixed-size comparisons are of new residual and attention mechanisms, not the depth, width and shape hyperparameters V4 refers to, so they are the study's own method compared with others, not a test of V4. Fig. 2 and Fig. 11 show loss falling with size and tokens, but give no fit or exponent.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly right. The authors conclude that value residual connections (ResFormer) improve information propagation and validation loss, matching Transformer loss with about 16% fewer parameters and 20% fewer training tokens. They conclude that SVFormer roughly halves the KV cache at a small loss cost that depends on sequence length and learning rate. They draw no conclusion about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes and evaluates alternative Transformer residual architectures rather than reproducing the scaling-law measurements or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that SVFormer performance varies with sequence length, learning rate and cumulative learning rate; ResFormer performance also varies with residual configuration and λ settings. These findings concern the paper's proposed architectures, not scaling-law fit choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding value residual connections shifts the loss-vs-size and loss-vs-data curves. ResFormer matches Transformer loss with 16.11% fewer parameters and 20.3% fewer tokens (Fig. 2, 82M–468M on 20B tokens). SVFormer needs 12.2% more parameters (Fig. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architectural modifications beyond shape hyperparameters can shift the scaling curve by a constant effective-parameter or effective-data factor at small scale (82M–1.6B).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2024
record.problems: The paper states that computational constraints prevented experiments on larger-scale models. The architecture comparisons test selected configurations, and the reported validation losses have no uncertainty estimates. Scaling curves are presented without fitted exponents or prediction tests.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 and Table 5 contain flattened or ambiguous row-to-value associations in the supplied text, so their individual comparisons were not extracted. Figure 2's validation-loss scaling curves were not entered as power-law results because no fitted values or exponents are reported. Other plots and tables concern the proposed architectures but do not provide clearly assignable additional fixed-size architecture-loss results for V4.

untested.parts: No power-law fit. Loss-vs-size (82M–468M) and loss-vs-tokens curves are shown only to compare architectures.
Depth, width, heads and other shape hyperparameters are not varied at fixed parameter count. Only novel residual mechanisms are compared.
Downstream scores (Table 2) are for one size and one token count. There is no predictability analysis.
No comparison of fits or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'tests' link and its labels are removed. The rows compare the study's own architecture with baselines and ablations, not the shape hyperparameters of V4. The scaling-law use is instrumental: the dataset was sized via Kaplan's D ≥ 5000·N^0.74.

versions.untested_parts: The paper varies model size and training tokens and reports validation-loss curves, but does not test whether those curves follow power laws, fit exponents, or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits are used to predict the losses of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget is allocated between parameters and tokens, and no compute-optimal trend is fitted.
The comparisons concern selected residual and attention variants, mostly 8-layer 82M models; they do not sweep depth, width, or a wide range of architecture configurations.
The reported experiments are language-model pretraining; no other modality or listed training regime is tested.
Downstream results are reported for models at one stated size and training-token count, without testing predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The paper does not fit scaling-law exponents or compare alternative scaling-law fitting choices.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported validation losses range from 2.739 for Transformer to 2.681 for ResFormer-Plus; these selected variants show comparatively clustered losses, though they do not establish a wide architecture range (r1–r9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Some architectural choices worsen loss, including Identity Mapping at 3.137 versus 2.712 for Current Attention; the effect is not uniformly slight across the tested mappings (r10–r16).
